deliverable: Phase 2 Task 5: validated astronomical datasets and documented limitations
method: Re-read the committed Task 2 series and Task 3 terrain reference, recompute every azimuth/elevation with LunaNav's independent analytic model, compare the records with the committed Horizons reference fetch, and check coordinates, observer, units, UTC handling, continuity and cross-site geometry. Nothing is repaired or filled in.

sources.label: NASA JPL Horizons API (observer tables at coord@301)
NASA PGDA LOLA 5 m/pix site DEMs

task5_items.item: Confirm that all three site coordinates are valid.
Verify the Horizons observer location is on the Moon.
Check Sun and Earth position results.
Compare selected results against Horizons reference output.
Confirm UTC date and time handling.
Check data continuity across the mission interval.
Test the same site on different dates.
Test different sites at the same date and time.
Document any assumptions or known limitations.

checks.title: Site coordinates are valid and agree across files
checks.task5_item: Confirm that all three site coordinates are valid.
checks.detail: 3 candidates validated: finite coordinates, a recorded source, inside their PGDA DEM footprint, and the same point in the Task 2 series.

checks.title: Horizons was asked for a lunar-surface observer
checks.task5_item: Verify the Horizons observer location is on the Moon.
checks.detail: Every query uses CENTER='coord@301' (the Moon, body 301), COORD_TYPE='GEODETIC', an altitude of a few km above the mean sphere, and the recorded site coordinate; the reference fetch echoes that same observer.

checks.title: Sun and Earth positions agree with an independent model
checks.task5_item: Check Sun and Earth position results.
checks.detail: All records recomputed with LunaNav's Meeus model from the same site coordinates; Horizons (light-time, physical libration) and the analytic model (neither) share no code.

checks.title: Committed values reproduce an independent Horizons fetch
checks.task5_item: Compare selected results against Horizons reference output.
checks.detail: 180 selected rows from a 12 h Horizons fetch over both mission windows, compared at the exact hourly timestamps in the series.

checks.title: Angles are degrees and distances are kilometres
checks.detail: Angles are degrees (the radian hypothesis is rejected by a wide margin) and ranges are kilometres at the physical Sun and Moon-Earth distances.

checks.title: Every timestamp is UTC, ISO-8601 and on the mission grid
checks.task5_item: Confirm UTC date and time handling.
checks.detail: Timestamps are ISO-8601 with Z, round-trip through the UTC parser, sit exactly on the configured landing date plus 7 days, and are one hour apart.

checks.title: No gaps or jumps across either mission interval
checks.task5_item: Check data continuity across the mission interval.
checks.detail: Every hour is present with no duplicates, and the largest hour-to-hour change is what the analytic geometry predicts (no swapped, repeated or interpolated rows).

checks.title: Each site's two mission windows are distinct and consistent
checks.task5_item: Test the same site on different dates.
checks.detail: The same observer point is used in both windows, the windows start ten days apart, and the Sun/Earth geometry differs in each as the model predicts.

checks.title: The three sites are three different observers
checks.task5_item: Test different sites at the same date and time.
checks.detail: At identical timestamps the sites differ by the amount their separation, latitude and elevation predict - the values were computed per observer, not shared.

checks.title: Assumptions and limitations are written down and complete
checks.task5_item: Document any assumptions or known limitations.
checks.detail: All ten Task 5 items are mapped to a check, ten limitations and seven assumptions are recorded here and in docs/VALIDATION.md.
A fresh 1 h fetch at each site's initial window start reproduces the committed records at the same timestamps.
Horizons echoed the observer it used for every live query.
The re-fetched reference table matches the previously committed one row for row.

assumptions: Longitude is selenographic east-positive in [-180, 180); Horizons receives the same meridian as 0-360 deg.
Heights are metres above the 1737.4 km IAU mean sphere; the Moon has no geoid.
The observer is the site point plus a 2 m antenna/eye height above the LOLA surface sample.
Elevation is apparent, airless and terrain-free: the geometric horizon, with no atmospheric refraction.
UTC is used everywhere; UTC -> TT for the analytic model uses the fixed 69.184 s offset valid for 2026-2030.
Hourly sampling is adequate to validate the data, not to time sunrise/Earthrise; Phase 3 refines edges.
Horizons applies light-time and aberration to the apparent position; the analytic model omits them.

limitations.impact: LunaNav verifies that the committed values reproduce Horizons and agree with an independent model. It cannot prove Horizons' own ephemeris is correct; Horizons remains the reference.
Meeus' truncated series omits physical libration, light-time and aberration. Agreement of a few hundredths of a degree is expected; a sub-arcsecond disagreement is not claimed.
Every elevation here is above the local flat horizon. A Sun or Earth at +0.5 deg can still be hidden by the 6-13 deg LOLA skylines in data/reference/site_terrain.json; Phase 3 applies them.
The series is hourly and the reference fetch is 12-hourly. A value at an un-sampled minute is not validated by either; Phase 3 interpolates and must say so.

A 2 m observer is assumed for all three sites. A real lander's camera, antenna or solar panel sits at a different height, which changes the geometric horizon by ~0.0005 deg per km and the terrain horizon much more.

Elevations are a 125 m-window median of a 5 m/pixel LOLA DEM, not a surveyed datum. The 0.3 m RMS height uncertainty is small next to the 5 m pixel, but the point itself is a study coordinate, not a certified landing pad.

Moon Mean Earth / Polar Axis, planetocentric, with the 1.54242 deg lunar-equator inclination in the analytic model. PA vs ME differences (~0.5 km at the surface) and any future IAU frame change are below the stated tolerances but not zero.
Physically correct for the Moon, but it means these elevations are not comparable with Earth-based observing conventions.
Sun elevation is illumination geometry, never electrical power; Earth elevation is line-of-sight geometry, never a communication link or data rate.
Only the three mission candidates and the two mission windows are validated. Custom coordinates and other dates reuse the same code but are not covered by this report.
